To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the Korean-made factor VIII concentrates were contaminated with HIV-1 subtype-B viruses and caused HIV-1 infection in hemophiliacs in Korea.

the phylogenetic analysis showed that the HIV-1 pol gene sequences from three plasma donors were clustered with 12 and 8 Korean hemophiliac patients, respectively, and were distinct from the 71 local control subjects.
the Korean-made clotting factors contaminated with HIV-1 were the major source of HIV-1 infection in Korean hemophiliac patients.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the phylogeny and evolution of HIV-1 in Korean hemophiliac patients and plasma donors.
the molecular epidemiology of HIV-1 in the Korean hemophiliac population.
the phylogenetic analysis of the pol gene of HIV-1 in the Korean hemophiliac and plasma donor populations, and provides further information on the molecular epidemiology of HIV-1 infection in Korea
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the outbreak was caused by the Korean-made factor.
the Korean-made factor VIII was contaminated by the plasma of donors O and P.
the HIV-1 viruses from donors O and P were transmitted to hemophiliacs in Korea, whereas those from donor R were not.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
Korean-made factor VIII was contaminated by HIV-1 from three cash-paid plasma donations, and that the three donors transmitted HIV-1 to 20 Korean hemophiliac patients.
donor P is a founder virus of the Korean subclades of HIV-1, and the Korean subclad of HIV-1 has a common ancestor with HIV-1 subtype A.
the Korean subclades of HIV-1 were divided into three subclades, KSB1, KSB2, and KSB3.
The main takeaway from our work is that
HIV-1 subtyping is important for the identification of the origin of HIV-1 infection in Korea.
the use of full-length pol genes is a powerful tool for the identification of viral strains that have caused an outbreak of HIV infection.
the use of frozen stored serum samples is useful for tracing the origin of HIV-1 infection in the past.
